{{Short description|American chemist (born 1942)}}
{{about|the chemist|other people named Robert Griffin|Robert Griffin (disambiguation)}}

'''Robert Guy Griffin''' (born 1942) is the Arthur Amos Noyes Professor of Chemistry<ref>{{cite web|title=Griffin Page|url=https://griffingroup.mit.edu/about-bob-griffin|work=MIT Department of Chemistry|accessdate=3 November 2022}}</ref>  and the director of the [[Francis Bitter]] Magnet Laboratory<ref>{{cite web|title=Francis Bitter Magnet Laboratory Page|url=http://web.mit.edu/fbml/|work=MIT|accessdate=30 January 2012}}</ref> at the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] (MIT). He is known for his work in high resolution, solid-state [[nuclear magnetic resonance]] (NMR) spectroscopy, a field where he has contributed many methods and approaches now widely used in applications of magic-angle spinning (MAS).<ref>V. Ladizhansky, R. S. Palani, M. Mardini and R. G. Griffin
Chemical Reviews 2024 Vol. 124 Issue 22 Pages 12844-12917.</ref> These include developing methods for heteronuclear decoupling and for measuring distances and torsion angles to determine molecular structures. In addition, he developed approaches for high-field [[dynamic nuclear polarization]] (DNP), which increases the sensitivity of MAS experiments by one or two orders of magnitude, primarily for the study of biological solids. He also pioneered methods for resolution enhancement via heteronuclear techniques for polarization transfer between nuclei (to enable structure determination of crystallised and aggregated proteins).His group used these methods to determine the initial structure of an amyloid fibril and more recently the structure of Aβ(1-40) and Aβ(1-42) fibrils, two of the primary pathological aggregates associated with [[Alzheimer's disease]].

Griffin's work has been recognized by election to the U. S. [[National Academy of Sciences]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.nasonline.org/news-and-multimedia/news/2021-nas-election.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210426172730/http://www.nasonline.org/news-and-multimedia/news/2021-nas-election.html|url-status=dead|archive-date=April 26, 2021|title=News from the National Academy of Sciences|date=26 April 2021|access-date=2 July 2021|quote=Newly elected members and their affiliations at the time of election are:  ...  Griffin, Robert G.; Arthur Amos Noyes Professor, department of chemistry, and director, Francis Bitter National Magnet Laboratory, Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Cambridge}}</ref> and the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]].<ref>https://www.amacad.org/person/robert-guy-griffin</ref>  He received the Günther Laukien Prize for NMR research in 2007,<ref>{{cite web|title=Laukien Prize Past Recipients (2007)|url=http://www.enc-conference.org/LaukienRecipients/PastRecipients/2007RobertGGriffin/tabid/75/Default.aspx|work=Experimental Nuclear Magnetic Resonance Conference|accessdate=30 January 2012|url-status=dead|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20100515060756/http://www.enc-conference.org/LaukienRecipients/PastRecipients/2007RobertGGriffin/tabid/75/Default.aspx|archivedate=15 May 2010}}</ref> the ISMAR (International Society of Magnetic Resonance ) Prize in 2010,<ref>{{cite web|title=ISMAR Prize|url=http://www.ismar.org/ismar-prize|work=International Society for Magnetic Resonance|accessdate=30 January 2012|url-status=dead|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20110218091517/http://www.ismar.org/ismar-prize|archivedate=18 February 2011}}</ref> the EB Wilson Award of
